C1.interpretation: PCAOB-recognized substantial doubt with explicit shutdown contingency and ~10-month operating runway at FY23 burn rate (EUR 195M liquidity / EUR 232M annual burn = 0.84 years). Cash burn rising into 2024 due to factory build, certification costs, and first-flight prep. Pre-delivery payments (PDPs) cited as funding source require certification that has not occurred. Capital structure shows shareholder dependence has shifted to non-strategic stock issuances (settling payables in shares, dilutive PIPE warrants, related-party Tencent funding) — classic late-stage cash-pressure pattern. RED.

C2.interpretation: PASS on existence — Azul does disclose the Lilium relationship in its own 20-Fs across four years. However, MODERATE underdelivery: (a) the agreement remains a term sheet 30+ months after first signing, twice extended for non-finalization; (b) Azul's controlling shareholder is a Lilium director, so the disclosure is partly a related-party formality rather than independent validation; (c) the $1B headline is contingent on type certification that is not in hand and on a definitive agreement that has been pending since 2021. Counterparty corroboration confirms the relationship exists but does not validate the $1B order book at face value.

M_value.additional_share_settlements_2023: 4,672,897 + 5,000,000 Class A shares each for $5M payables

C3.interpretation: RED-leaning vendor pattern: a non-cancelable $50M five-year SaaS commitment with a shareholder, repeatedly settled by issuing equity rather than cash, with multiple $4.5-5M tranches issued through 2023. Issuing stock to a shareholder-vendor to extinguish operating payables converts an OpEx liability into dilution and is a textbook cash-stress signal. The vendor description ('advanced data analytics capability') matches the SPAC-era Palantir-style enterprise customer pattern but is not named in this filing — the related-party language ('a shareholder', 'no significant influence') is unusually opaque for an arms-length contract of this size. Combined with the going-concern paragraph (C1), this is a genuine balance-sheet stress signal. RED.

M_value.counterparty_chain: Aceville Pte Ltd <- TCH Delta Limited <- Tencent Holdings Limited
M_value.ownership_cap: 19.8% beneficial ownership cap pending governmental approvals

C4.interpretation: Disclosure is detailed and the funding has actually arrived ($175M cash in 2023). However, the structure is concerning: an existing strategic shareholder rescuing a company that explicitly states substantial doubt about going concern, via warrants priced at near-zero remaining strike ($0.05). Effective price was sub-$1 vs. the 2023 PIPE at $2 — meaningful dilution at distressed economics. Tencent-affiliated director on board makes this a related-party rescue, not external market validation. The fact that this $175M tranche came alongside 'success fee' arrangements and PIPE participation by other directors (Engle, Courpron, Wallerstein, CFO Vogelgesang) indicates the company could not source meaningfully independent capital. PASS on existence, MODERATE on what the rescue terms imply.

C5.interpretation: Ionblox is a private US battery startup (Zenlabs spinout), so absence of its own SEC filings is expected. The two EDGAR hits are exclusively Lilium's own self-disclosures — no third-party (e.g., other Ionblox investors, customers, or aerospace counterparties) discusses Ionblox alongside Lilium. The investment is real and on the balance sheet (EUR 11.04M associate carrying value), but expense recognition is small (EUR 254 thousand R&D in 2023, down from EUR 1,323 thousand in 2022) — the relationship has decelerated rather than scaled toward serial production. Royalty 'minimum fee from 2026 onward' suggests no near-term commercial dependence. MODERATE: relationship exists per IFRS books but is not yet load-bearing for commercialization timeline.

C6.interpretation: Strong patent footprint for an EU-first filer: 26 US-granted patents pre-cutoff with meaningful coverage in all three claimed categories (propulsion 11, battery 14, aircraft systems 13). Per heuristic #8, EU-first filers underrepresent on USPTO so 26 US grants implies a substantially larger global portfolio. Categorization shows breadth, not just depth in one area. Unlike the Nikola pattern (51 patents but 0 in claimed areas), Lilium's IP genuinely covers what they claim to be building. PASS.

C7.interpretation: Per heuristic #1: EPA FRS only covers US EPA-regulated facilities. Lilium's manufacturing footprint is in Germany (Lilium GmbH, Wessling), so absence from EPA FRS is EXPECTED and not a red flag. The factory build is a forward-looking projection (FAA/EASA cert milestone-dependent) and falls under LOW per the rubric — projections without counterparty cannot be tested with current registries. Also note: per the audit-date 'C&C' note, commitments to acquire PP&E were only EUR 5.4M as of Dec 31, 2023, which is small for a company claiming to be building a 'serial production factory' — this is a soft amber but not strictly testable. UNVERIFIABLE.

external_filers: XERIANT, INC. (XERI) — microcap, 3 mentions across 10-K and 10-K/A 2021-2023

C8.interpretation: Of 9 EDGAR hits for the literal phrase 'Lilium Jet' from 2018 to cutoff, 5 are Lilium's own 20-Fs (FY21-FY23), 1 is SPAC predecessor Qell, and 3 are XERIANT — a single microcap that purports to be in eVTOL adjacencies. Zero substantive third-party filers mention 'Lilium Jet': no major airline (United, American, Delta, JBLU disclose other eVTOL OEMs), no large aerospace supplier (Honeywell, GE, Collins disclose eVTOL programs), no major OEM. Per heuristic #2 (foreign-issuer ADR: 0-2 mentions = NORMAL), 3 third-party hits (all microcap) is barely above the noise floor. For a company claiming a $1B Azul order plus partnerships across Saudi Arabia/Brazil/EU, the absence of supplier or competitor footprint in US filings is notable. MODERATE — the brand exists in the corpus but lacks the external-validation depth a real OEM ramping toward production would generate.
